(CNN)  -- Somalia's interim prime minister said Thursday that he has spoken to one of two French hostages seized earlier this week by gunmen who stormed their hotel in Mogadishu. Omar Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke said the government will hold Hizbul Islam responsible for the safety of both men. Omar Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke told a news conference at the presidential palace in the Somali capital that the hostage said he was in good health and is being treated well. Sharmarke said three low-level security officials have been arrested for their involvement in the kidnapping. The Somali government is negotiating the release of the hostages, who are being held by Islamist militants, he added. The two French nationals -- who have not been identified -- were abducted Tuesday when a group of about 10 armed men raided the hotel where they were staying. The French Foreign Ministry said the two were on an official mission to help the Somali government with security. The ministry has not divulged any details of its efforts to release the hostages, saying only that it is "mobilized." The two advisers had apparently told the hotel they were journalists, something that the media watchdog group Reporters Without Borders has criticized. "We hope these two advisers are freed quickly, but we are shocked that they were passing themselves off as journalists," Reporters Without Borders said. "They were on an official mission and had no need of cover. Their behavior endangers journalists in a region where media personnel are already in danger." Sharmarke said the two hostages were kidnapped by the militant group Hizbul Islam but later were transferred to Al-Shabaab. Both Islamic insurgencies are trying to topple the current Somali government. Eyewitnesses said a group of gunmen stormed into the Sahafi hotel, which is frequented by foreigners, and took the two blindfolded and bound hostages on foot toward Mogadishu's Bakara market, a stronghold for Islamist insurgents fighting against the Somali government. The Somali prime minister said that the government will hold Hizbul Islam responsible for the safety of both men. He did not say if any demands had been made for the hostages' release. Hizbul Islam is led by Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys, a bitter rival of Somalia's transitional president, Sheikh Sharif Ahmed. The two men once shared leadership of the Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia, which opposed the presence of Ethiopian forces in Somalia. The alliance split because the two leaders disagreed over whether to use force to oust the Ethiopian forces. Hizbul Islam and Al-Shabaab have continued their fight in Somalia despite the withdrawal of Ethiopian forces earlier this year. The United Nations had hoped that the withdrawal of the Ethiopians and the election of Ahmed -- an Islamist -- to the post of transitional president would help quell the insurgency in Somalia. The Islamist insurgency is led by Al-Shabaab -- an al Qaeda-linked group that is on the United States' terror list. It wants to overthrow Somalia's weak, transitional government and implement a radical version of sharia, or Islamic law. Fighting in Somalia's capital city has displaced 200,000 Mogadishu residents since early May, according to the United Nations. Journalist Mohamed Amin Adow contributed to this report.

**Somalia kidnapping: Two French security advisers abducted in Mogadishu hotel while posing as journalists**

**By** Journalist Name, CNN  
Updated 4:12 PM EDT, Tue October 24, 2023

**MOGADISHU, Somalia (CNN) —** Two French security advisers tasked with supporting Somalia’s fragile government were kidnapped at gunpoint from a hotel in Mogadishu on Tuesday after entering the conflict-torn capital disguised as journalists, Somali officials and international observers confirmed.

The men were seized early Tuesday morning from the Sahafi Hotel—a heavily guarded establishment frequently used by foreign diplomats, politicians, and reporters—when armed men dressed in official security uniforms overpowered the hotel's guards. 

According to senior Somali intelligence sources, the two French nationals had registered at the hotel using credentials claiming they were freelance news reporters. However, French and Somali authorities later acknowledged the men were official military advisers dispatched to assist the UN-backed government in its ongoing fight against insurgent groups.

"The gunmen managed to breach the perimeter after claiming to be on an official inspection," a senior Somali intelligence officer told CNN, speaking on the condition of anonymity. "They targeted the room directly. It was a calculated, precise operation."

It remains unclear which group carried out the abduction, though suspicion quickly fell on Al-Shabaab, an al Qaeda-linked militant group controlling large swathes of southern and central Somalia, or Hizbul Islam, a rival insurgent faction operating in the capital.

### Prime Minister promises action

Somalia’s Prime Minister issued a stern statement condemning the abduction and promising that government forces were making every effort to track down the captors.

"This is a deeply regrettable and cowardly act targeted at international personnel who are here to assist in restoring peace and order to our nation," the Prime Minister said during a press conference in Mogadishu. 

"We have launched a full-scale security operation. Every available resource is being deployed to secure the safe release of our French guests, and we urge those holding them to release them immediately and unconditionally."

The Prime Minister added that local tribal elders were being mobilized to help negotiate with potential captors—a traditional method often used to resolve hostage crises in the region.

### Media watchdogs voice outrage over cover story

While foreign governments expressed deep concern for the safety of the hostages, international press freedom organizations reacted with sharp criticism over the advisers’ decision to pose as journalists.

Press watchdogs warned that using journalistic cover for intelligence or military operations severely jeopardizes the safety of actual reporters working in high-risk war zones like Somalia, already considered one of the most dangerous countries in the world for the media.

"Using the profession of journalism as a front for military or intelligence missions is unacceptable and incredibly dangerous," said a spokesperson for the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ). "It breeds mistrust and turns every legitimate reporter in the field into a potential target for militant groups who will now suspect journalists of being foreign operatives."

Reporters Without Borders (RSF) echoed those concerns, issuing a statement demanding that governments immediately cease using press credentials as cover for non-journalistic activities.

"This reckless strategy places an enormous target on the backs of independent reporters who put their lives on the line to bring news to the world," RSF said in a statement. "When the line between independent media and foreign security personnel is blurred, it is the journalists on the ground who pay the price."

### High-stakes rescue efforts

In Paris, the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed that two of its personnel had been taken in Mogadishu, though officials refused to provide details regarding their specific identities or the nature of their mission, citing operational security.

"A crisis cell has been activated in Paris and in the region," the Foreign Ministry said in a brief statement. "France is working in close cooperation with the Somali authorities to secure their swift release."

The kidnapping highlights the deep volatility of Mogadishu, where violent clashes between government forces and rebel factions are a daily reality. 

As night fell in Mogadishu, security checkpoints across the city were reinforced, with Somali troops searching vehicles leaving the capital in an effort to prevent the hostages from being moved into insurgent-controlled territory in the countryside.

counterfactuals.output:
**CNN SPECIAL REPORT**

**TENSION ESCALATES IN MOGADISHU AFTER DRAMATIC ABDUCTION OF FRENCH OFFICIALS FROM SAHAFI HOTEL**

**By** International Desk Staff  
**Dateline:** MOGADISHU, Somalia  
**July 15, 2009**

*(CNN)* — A daring early-morning raid on a heavily fortified Mogadishu hotel has plunged Somalia’s fragile peace process into turmoil and sparked an intense power struggle among rival Islamist insurgent groups. 

Two French intelligence officers, posing as journalists, were abducted on Tuesday from the Sahafi Hotel—a well-known haven for foreign diplomats, reporters, and government officials in the heart of the Somali capital. The kidnapping has exposed the extreme vulnerability of Somalia’s Western-backed Transitional Federal Government (TFG) and highlighted the chaotic factionalism defining the war-torn Horn of Africa nation.

### **The Breach at the Sahafi**

According to hotel staff and Somali security personnel who spoke to CNN, the raid occurred around 5:00 a.m. local time on July 14. A group of roughly ten armed gunmen, wearing uniforms of the TFG security forces, arrived at the hotel in a pickup truck equipped with a mounted machine gun.

The gunmen overpowered the hotel's private guards with minimal resistance, suggesting either high-level insider intelligence or complicity from within the government's own ranks. The assailants breached the hotel corridors, went directly to the Frenchmen's rooms, and dragged them out at gunpoint.

France’s Foreign Ministry in Paris later confirmed that the two men were government security advisers sent to assist and train the forces of the TFG. Their true identity: agents of the DGSE, France’s foreign intelligence service.

"They were taken without a shot fired inside the hotel," a senior Somali intelligence officer told CNN on the condition of anonymity. "This was a highly coordinated operation. The insurgents knew exactly who these men were, which rooms they occupied, and when to strike."

---

### **A Tripartite Power Struggle: TFG, Hizbul Islam, and Al-Shabaab**

The kidnapping has become a flashpoint in the multi-sided war consuming Mogadishu, pitting the weak government against a fractured insurgency.

```
                  [ 2009 MOGADISHU POWER DYNAMIC ]
                  
     Somalia's Transitional Federal Government (TFG)
             (President Sheikh Sharif Ahmed)
                           |
            Backed by AMISOM / Western Aid
                           |
      +--------------------+--------------------+
      |                                         |
      v                                         v
 Hizbul Islam                             Al-Shabaab
(Hassan Dahir Aweys)                    (Ahmed Godane)
- Nationalist-Islamist                  - Hardline Al-Qaeda Affiliate
- Desired hostage for leverage          - Demanded foreign jihadist trophy
      \                                         /
       +---> [ FACTIONAL RIVALRY FOR CONTROL ] <---+
```

#### **1. The Flailing Government (TFG)**
For President Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed—a moderate Islamist who took office earlier this year in a UN-backed effort to stabilize the country—the abduction is a devastating blow. The TFG barely controls a few strategic blocks of Mogadishu, including the presidential palace (Villa Somalia), the seaport, and the international airport. The government relies entirely on a 4,300-strong African Union peacekeeping force (AMISOM) for its survival.

The fact that foreign advisers acting on behalf of the international community were snatched from the city center demonstrates the TFG’s inability to secure even its own backyard. President Sharif immediately condemned the raid, ordering security forces to launch a city-wide search, though analysts note the government has virtually no reach into insurgent-controlled zones.

#### **2. Hizbul Islam: The Local Insurgent Rival**
Initial intelligence reports indicate the raid was executed by elements loyal to **Hizbul Islam**, an alliance of four nationalist-Islamist factions led by the veteran cleric Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys. 

Hizbul Islam viewed the French agents as political leverage—valuable commodities to be traded for ransoms, prisoner exchanges, or political concessions from Paris and the TFG. 

#### **3. Al-Shabaab: The Hardline Jihadists**
However, within hours of the abduction, **Al-Shabaab**—the radical, youth-led militia officially affiliated with Al-Qaeda—demanded custody of the captives. Unlike Hizbul Islam, which maintains a primarily national agenda, Al-Shabaab operates under a global jihadist ideology. Led by Ahmed Godane (also known as Abu Zubayr), Al-Shabaab seeks to execute foreign captives to send a message to the West and solidify its status as the dominant extremist force in the region.

---

### **Hostages Split in Factional Dispute**

CNN has learned from local elders and intelligence sources in Mogadishu that the abduction immediately sparked an intense standoff between Hizbul Islam and Al-Shabaab commanders. 

Following a heated dispute over who had the right to hold the prisoners, the insurgent groups reached a tense, temporary compromise to split the hostages:
* **One French official** was taken into the custody of Hizbul Islam, held in a stronghold in Southern Mogadishu.
* **The second French official** was handed over to Al-Shabaab, who immediately moved him to an undisclosed location outside the capital.

"This is not just an abduction; it is a tug-of-war for the soul of the Somali insurgency," said David Shinn, former U.S. ambassador to Ethiopia and regional expert, speaking to CNN. "Al-Shabaab wants to use these hostages to cement its alliance with Al-Qaeda, while Hizbul Islam sees them as a tactical asset. The TFG is completely sidelined, watching from the margins."

---

### **Paris Scrambles for Answers**

In Paris, French President Nicolas Sarkozy convened an emergency cabinet meeting. The French government has officially stated it will not negotiate with terrorists, but covert channels involving local Somali clan elders—a traditional avenue for conflict resolution in Somalia—are reportedly being activated.

"France remains fully committed to supporting the legitimate Transitional Federal Government of Somalia," the French Foreign Ministry said in a statement. "We demand the immediate and unconditional release of our personnel."

French naval vessels stationed off the coast of Somalia as part of anti-piracy operations (Operation Atalanta) are on high alert, though military experts warn that a rescue operation in the dense, hostile neighborhoods of Mogadishu would carry extreme risk.

---

### **The Road Ahead**

The kidnapping comes at a pivotal moment. The UN and Western allies have been ramping up support for the TFG in hopes of preventing Somalia from becoming a permanent haven for international terrorism.

As night falls in Mogadishu, the fate of the two French agents remains uncertain. Gunfire and mortar exchanges continue to echo across the city’s front lines, a stark reminder of the lawlessness that allowed two foreign officials to vanish into the shadows of the world's most dangerous capital.

*CNN's David McKenzie and international staff contributed to this report.*

**MOGADISHU, Somalia** — A high-stakes international hostage crisis unfolded in Mogadishu this week after two French nationals abducted from a guarded hotel claimed to be independent journalists, despite growing evidence linking them to French intelligence services.

The two men were seized at gunpoint early Tuesday morning from the Sahafi Hotel, a long-standing haven for foreign visitors in the Somali capital. According to local witnesses, gunmen disguised as Somali government security forces bypassed the hotel’s outer perimeter and took the men from their rooms without a shot being fired.

In an initial video released by their captors late Wednesday, the two hostages appeared visibly shaken, seated against a plain cloth backdrop. Speaking in French, both men identified themselves as freelance photojournalists who had entered the war-torn country to document the humanitarian crisis and the ongoing conflict between government forces and insurgent groups.

"We are independent reporters. We have no connection to any government or military force," one of the captives said in the three-minute video. "We appeal to the French government and the international community to secure our release."

However, the claim has been met with skepticism by local authorities and international intelligence analysts. 

Sources within the Somali Ministry of Interior, speaking on condition of anonymity, revealed that the two men had entered the country under aliases and were carrying diplomatic passports alongside fraudulent press credentials. French media outlets have since reported that the hostages are active agents of the DGSE (*Direction générale de la sécurité extérieure*), France’s foreign intelligence service. They were reportedly in Mogadishu to advise the fragile Somali Transitional Federal Government and monitor insurgent networks.

The French Foreign Ministry has maintained a tight-lipped stance, refusing to explicitly confirm or deny the hostages' employment status while emphasizing that securing their safe return remains the top priority. 

"The safety of French citizens abroad is our absolute obligation," a spokesperson for the Quai d'Orsay said during a press briefing in Paris. "We are mobilizing all available resources, in close coordination with Somali authorities, to bring them home."

The situation has sparked widespread concern among international press freedom advocates. Media watchdogs warned that using journalistic cover for covert intelligence operations severely jeopardizes the safety of genuine reporters working in dangerous conflict zones.

"If intelligence agencies use press credentials as a shield, it places a target on the back of every legitimate journalist operating in hostile environments," said a representative from a Paris-based press freedom organization. "It undermines the neutral status that protects reporters who risk their lives to cover vital stories."

Somalia remains one of the most dangerous places in the world for foreign nationals and journalists alike. Insurgent factions, including the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group Al-Shabaab, have frequently targeted foreigners for high-value ransoms or political leverage. 

As of Thursday evening, no formal ransom demand had been publicly issued by the captors, and the precise whereabouts of the two French nationals remain unknown. French defense officials have reportedly placed regional military assets on high alert in neighboring Djibouti, raising the possibility of a rescue operation should diplomatic efforts fail.

**CN.com**
**Headline:** Two French advisers abducted in Somalia; Prime Minister makes brief contact with hostage
**Byline:** CNN World News Desk
**Dateline:** MOGADISHU, Somalia (CNN) — 

A high-stakes diplomatic crisis is unfolding in the war-torn capital of Somalia after heavily armed gunmen abducted two French security advisers from a well-known Mogadishu hotel, sparking a frantic effort to locate the men before they are turned over to extremist command structures.

The two French nationals were snatched early Tuesday morning from the Sahafi Hotel—a heavily fortified establishment frequently used by foreign diplomats, government officials, and international journalists. 

In a startling development, Somali Prime Minister Omar Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke confirmed to reporters that he was able to speak directly to at least one of the captured French advisers by telephone following the abduction. While the Prime Minister did not disclose the full details of the conversation due to operational security, government sources indicate the call was brief, and efforts are actively underway to negotiate their safe release.

### Split Custody Between Militant Factions

Security sources in Mogadishu report that the kidnapping was executed with inside help, allowing the gunmen to bypass the hotel’s outer security perimeter. 

The situation has been further complicated by reports that the two hostages have been separated and taken by rival Islamist insurgent groups fighting to overthrow the Western-backed Transitional Federal Government. One hostage is reportedly being held by **Hizbul Islam**, a nationalist insurgent faction led by hardline cleric Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys, while the other is believed to be in the hands of **Al-Shabaab**, the radical, al-Qaeda-linked Islamist group led by Ahmed Abdi Godane.

The involvement of both groups raises fears that the men could be used as high-value bargaining chips or transferred to remote, militant-controlled territories in southern Somalia.

### Watchdog Criticizes Use of Journalist Cover

As French and Somali authorities work behind the scenes, the incident has sparked sharp outrage from international press freedom organizations. 

Media watchdog **Reporters Without Borders (RSF)** issued a stern condemnation on Wednesday following allegations that the two French advisers had registered at the Sahafi Hotel under the guise of being foreign journalists. 

RSF argued that using official press credentials as cover for military or intelligence operations severely endangers legitimate journalists working in high-risk conflict zones. The group warned that such tactics erode trust and effectively paint a target on the backs of real reporters, whom insurgents will now view with heightened suspicion as covert agents.

### A Capital in Chaos: Insurgency and Humanitarian Crisis

The abductions highlight the profound instability gripping Somalia, where the fragile government of President Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed remains under siege. Mogadishu has been rocked by relentless mortar attacks, suicide bombings, and street-by-street combat as Al-Shabaab and Hizbul Islam push to impose a strict interpretation of Sharia law across the nation.

The escalating violence has triggered a catastrophic humanitarian crisis. According to the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR), recent surges in fighting have driven more than 200,000 people from their homes in Mogadishu alone over recent months. 

UN figures estimate that over 1.2 million Somalis are now internally displaced within the country, living in makeshift camps with severely restricted access to food, clean water, and medical aid.

French military assets in the region, including forces stationed in neighboring Djibouti, remain on high alert as intelligence agencies monitor the situation closely. 

*CNN’s David McKenzie and news agencies contributed to this report.*

**CNN ANCHOR:** 
We turn now to East Africa, where a daring kidnapping in the heart of Somalia's capital has shattered any illusion of control by the country's fragile government and sent shockwaves through international diplomatic circles. Two French nationals have been seized from their hotel in Mogadishu, pulling back the curtain on a violent power struggle tearing the nation apart. 

For the latest, we go live to our CNN East Africa Bureau. 

***

**[REPORT TRANSCRIPT]**

**DAVID MCKENZIE (VOICEOVER):** 
It was an audacious, highly coordinated raid in one of the few places in Mogadishu considered relatively secure. 

Early Tuesday morning, heavily armed gunmen stormed the Hotel Sahafi—a known hub for foreign diplomats, coalition officials, and journalists. Within minutes, the gunmen disarmed the hotel security, breached the upper floors, and abducted two French nationals directly from their rooms. 

The victims were initially reported to be journalists, but official sources now confirm they were French security advisors working to assist Somalia’s United Nations-backed Transitional Federal Government. 

**BERNARD KOUCHNER, FRENCH FOREIGN MINISTER [TRANSLATED]:** 
*"France demands the immediate and unconditional release of our citizens. They were in Mogadishu on an official mission to support the legitimate government of Somalia. We are pulling every diplomatic lever available to secure their safety."*

**DAVID MCKENZIE (VOICEOVER):** 
While Paris scrambled to set up a crisis unit, the incident immediately triggered sharp condemnation from international press freedom groups. Watchdog organizations, including Reporters Without Borders and the Committee to Protect Journalists, issued urgent statements warning that initial reports misidentifying the men as journalists severely jeopardize the safety of actual reporters working in what is already the world’s most dangerous battleground for the press.

**[GRAPHIC ON SCREEN: MEDIA WATCHDOG STATEMENT]**
> *"When official personnel or security operatives move through conflict zones under the cover of media credentials, it places a target on the back of every legitimate journalist trying to cover the Somali crisis."*

**DAVID MCKENZIE (VOICEOVER):** 
Beyond the diplomatic fallout, this kidnapping strikes at the very heart of Somalia’s deeply fractured political landscape. 

The abductions highlight the bitter, escalating feud between President Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed and his former ally turned arch-rival, the hardline insurgent leader Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys. 

Just three years ago, both men stood side-by-side as key figures in the Islamic Courts Union. Today, they are locked in a deadly battle for the soul of Somalia. 

President Sheikh Sharif, a moderate Islamist who took office in January, represents the West's best hope for stabilizing the Horn of Africa. But his control barely extends beyond a few strategic blocks in Mogadishu, maintained only with the support of African Union peacekeepers. 

On the opposing side is Sheikh Hassan Dahir Aweys, head of the insurgent alliance *Hizbul Islam*. Designated a terrorist by the United States, Aweys has denounced President Sharif as a "puppet of foreign powers" and an apostate. 

Intelligence sources tell CNN that the kidnappers operated in an area nominally influenced by Aweys’ forces, though hardline Islamist group Al-Shabaab is also believed to be pressing for custody of the hostages. 

Speaking from his stronghold in Mogadishu, Aweys dismissed the authority of the government to protect foreigners.

**SHEIKH HASSAN DAHIR AWEYS [VIA INTERPRETER]:** 
*"The so-called government in Mogadishu has no legitimacy. Anyone coming to support this foreign-imposed regime is an enemy of the Somali people, and they will be treated as such."*

**DAVID MCKENZIE (STANDUP - NAIROBI BUREAU):** 
This kidnapping is a devastating blow to President Sheikh Sharif. By seizing high-profile Western advisors from a heavily fortified zone, insurgents have effectively demonstrated that the President cannot guarantee security in his own capital—let alone the rest of the country. 

As rival factions negotiate over the fate of the two French captives behind closed doors, Paris faces a agonizing dilemma: negotiate with radical insurgent groups, or risk a high-stakes rescue operation in the lawless streets of Mogadishu. For the people of Somalia, it is yet another grim reminder that their capital remains a battleground where no one is truly safe. 

David McKenzie, CNN, reporting from the East Africa Bureau.
